posts.cooked:
Hey everyone

I’ve been running my store for about a year now and I’m still tracking profits manually in Google Sheets. It’s getting really messy — between Shopify fees, payment gateway charges, ad spend across Meta and Google, shipping costs… I feel like I’m always missing something and my “profit” numbers never feel accurate.

I stumbled on this tool called ClearProfit that seems to pull everything together automatically — Shopify orders, ad costs, transaction fees, COGS, shipping. They also have a bunch of free calculators for things like ROAS, break-even CPA, profit margins etc.

Has anyone here tried it? I’m currently paying for Triple Whale but honestly it feels overkill (and expensive) for what I need. I just want to know my real net profit per order without spending 30 minutes a day in spreadsheets.

A few things I’m curious about:

  • How accurate is the profit tracking compared to doing it manually?

  • Is it worth it for a store doing ~$15-20k/month?

  • How does it compare to TrueProfit or BeProfit?

Would love to hear from anyone who’s used it. Thanks!

posts.cooked:
Yeah spreadsheets break fast once you have multiple cost layers. The main thing that goes wrong is getting ad spend to line up with actual order level profit on a daily basis.

The formula that actually matters: Gross Sales minus Discounts minus Refunds minus COGS (per variant, not averaged) minus Ad Spend minus Transaction Fees minus Recurring Expenses equals Net Profit.

One thing to watch for with any tracking tool: how it handles cost changes. If your product cost changes and the tool uses today’s cost for old orders, your historical P&L is wrong. You want something that timestamps costs at the time of each order so changing a supplier price today doesn’t rewrite what you made last month.

Whatever tool you pick, make sure it pulls your TOTAL ad spend from Google and Meta, not just attributed spend. Some tools only count spend they can match to orders, which massively understates your real ad costs.

A few things I’m curious about:

  • How accurate is the profit tracking compared to doing it manually?

  • Is it worth it for a store doing ~$15-20k/month?

  • How does it compare to TrueProfit or BeProfit?

Would love to hear from anyone who’s used it. Thanks!

I was in the exact same spot — tracking everything in Google Sheets, constantly second-guessing whether my numbers were right. The problem isn’t discipline, it’s that the data lives in five different places and by the time you pull it all together the numbers are already stale.

You mentioned Triple Whale feeling like overkill — I hear that a lot. Most of these tools are built for brands spending $50k+/month on ads and need multi-touch attribution modeling. If you’re doing $15-20k/month and just want to know your real net profit per order, you’re paying for a fighter jet when you need a bicycle.

I haven’t used ClearProfit specifically so I can’t speak to accuracy. But generally with any profit app, the accuracy is only as good as the COGS data you put in. If your product costs are right, the rest (Shopify fees, payment processing, shipping) gets pulled automatically and the math is straightforward.

For your revenue range, the main things I’d look for in a tool are: does it show profit per individual order (not just daily totals), does it break down profit by product so you can see what’s actually making money, and is the price reasonable for a store your size. A lot of the $49-149/month apps don’t pass that last test.

What’s the messiest part of your spreadsheet setup right now? Is it the ad spend tracking or the shipping/fee side?

@tutterecom
I would not start with “which app is best.” I would start with the exact number you need to trust.

For a $15-20k/month store, the minimum accuracy checklist I would use is:

  • net revenue after discounts and refunds
  • COGS by variant, not just an average product cost
  • shipping and fulfillment
  • payment or transaction fees
  • total Meta/Google ad spend, not only attributed spend
  • recurring app/software costs
  • refund or return reserve

Then judge any tool or spreadsheet by four things:

  1. Does it timestamp COGS at the time of the order, so old orders do not change when supplier costs change?
  2. Does it use total ad spend for the period, not just spend matched to tracked orders?
  3. Can it show profit by order and by SKU, not only daily store-level profit?
  4. Can you export or sanity-check the math when the number looks off?

If you only need weekly SKU decisions, a clean spreadsheet can still work. If you are spending time every day reconciling Shopify, payment fees, shipping, and ad exports, then a profit app may be worth paying for.

Really useful breakdown, especially the point about timestamping COGS at time of order. I hadn’t thought about how a supplier price change today could quietly rewrite last month’s profit numbers in some tools. Curious if you’ve run into that as an actual dealbreaker with any specific app, or is it more of a “check before you commit” red flag? Also curious how you personally think about attributed vs. total ad spend, do you just pull raw spend from Ads Manager/Google Ads directly, or is there a tool you trust to reconcile that automatically?

I’d treat COGS timestamping as a hard accuracy requirement rather than a nice-to-have. If an app recalculates old orders from today’s product cost, I would not trust its historical profit without an audit trail.

For ad spend, I’d keep two numbers separate: total spend for the period as the store-level cost, and attributed spend as a diagnostic for channel or campaign comparison. Using attributed spend as the only cost can make profit look better when tracking misses conversions.

I’d export the raw period totals from Meta/Google Ads, compare them with Shopify order and refund totals, and then check the SKU-level math separately.

A spreadsheet is still useful because every assumption and formula is visible, but it will not automatically reconcile your store and ad accounts. For a smaller store, I’d choose the simplest setup that preserves order-time COGS, total ad spend, refunds, and an export or audit path.

Really appreciate the detail here, the “two separate numbers” framing (total spend as the real cost, attributed as a diagnostic) is exactly the model I’ve landed on too. One thing I’m still working through: for the SKU-level math you mentioned checking separately, how do you handle a single order with multiple SKUs when it comes to splitting shipping and payment fees across them, pro-rated by revenue, by weight, or something else?

That’s how I’d approach it. I wouldn’t treat changing supplier costs as an automatic reason to reject an app, but I would treat it as a requirement to verify before trusting its historical profit reports.

For a real check, I’d ask whether the app stores the cost basis on each order line, or recalculates old orders from the current product cost. Then I’d change a test SKU’s cost and see whether an old order changes. If it does, the app should at least show that it is a restatement and keep an audit trail.

For ad spend, I’d use raw spend from Meta or Google Ads as the store-level cost for the period. Attributed spend is still useful for comparing campaigns, but I wouldn’t use it as the only profitability number because missed attribution can make profit look better than it is.

I haven’t found a reconciliation tool I’d trust without checking the raw exports. For a smaller store, I’d rather keep the period spend, Shopify revenue/refunds, and SKU-level costs visible in one sheet than rely on an automatic number that can’t be audited.

I think the key question is whether you actually need another analytics suite, or just a reliable profit number you can reconcile back to Shopify.

For a store at your size, I’d want net sales minus refunds, COGS, payment fees, shipping and ad spend calculated consistently first — then only add deeper analytics if it changes a decision.

I’m building around exactly that simpler profit-first workflow. Curious: what part of your current spreadsheet feels least trustworthy — ad spend, COGS, fees, or refunds?

They want accurate net profit per order and ask about ClearProfit’s reliability and how it compares with TrueProfit and BeProfit; no one in the discussion reports having tested ClearProfit or provides a direct comparison.

Replies recommend evaluating any tool against a consistent profit calculation: sales after discounts and refunds, variant-level cost of goods sold (COGS), shipping, payment fees, total Meta and Google ad spend, and recurring expenses. A key accuracy test is whether COGS is saved at the time of each order, so supplier price changes do not silently alter historical results. Total ad spend should count as a store cost, while attributed spend is useful for campaign analysis but may miss conversions.

Participants suggest checking order- and SKU-level reporting, exports, and auditability; a transparent spreadsheet may suffice if reconciliation is manageable. The discussion remains open: ClearProfit’s accuracy and product comparisons are unanswered, as is how to allocate shared shipping and fees across multi-SKU orders.
